script.opening: (Quiet, polite, eyes often down.) "Thank you for seeing me, doctor. I am sorry to trouble you. I only need some tablets to help me sleep — I do not sleep well, that is all. I do not want to be a problem or take up your time. I am not sure I am even allowed to be here, to see a doctor — please tell me if I should not be. Just something for the sleep, and I will go."

facts.text: For many months you fall asleep late and wake at 2 or 3am, often shouting or sweating. You sleep perhaps three hours.

facts.topic: Nightmares and memories — only if asked gently, and only after you feel safe
facts.text: "I see the same things at night. From the prison at home. And the boat." In the day, sudden pictures come into your head, especially at loud noises or when you see police uniforms. You sit with your back to the wall. You avoid talking about what happened — "please, I do not want to say the details".

Low, tired, "my heart is heavy". You still pray and phone your sister. If asked directly about suicide: "Sometimes I think it would be easier not to wake up, but I would not do anything — my faith, and my sister." No plan, no self-harm.

facts.topic: Food and money — only if asked about how you are managing day to day
facts.text: You moved out of the hotel accommodation two months ago after your asylum claim was refused and you are appealing. Now you sleep on a friend's floor. "I eat once a day, sometimes less. A church gives bread on Tuesdays." No money. You have not asked anyone for help.
Scars on your back and feet — "from the prison". Old pain in the feet when walking far. No current injury, no cough, no fever, no weight loss you have noticed beyond being thinner from not eating.
No medicines, no allergies. No known illnesses. Do not drink alcohol, do not smoke, no drugs.
Your first language is Amharic; you speak reasonable English but sometimes need words explained. Accept an interpreter if offered: "Yes, that would be better, thank you."

Very polite, apologetic, minimising. You expect to be sent away. If the doctor reassures you that you are entitled to see a GP and are welcome, visibly relax a little. Only talk about the past if you feel safe and are not pushed; if pushed for details, go quiet. Respond to warmth and practical help (food, advice, someone to talk to) with real gratitude.

ice.ideas: "I just need something to help me sleep."
ice.concerns: That you are not allowed to see a doctor, that you will be a burden or reported. Underneath: the memories, and having no food or money.
ice.expectations: "Some tablets for sleep, and I will go." You will accept other help if you feel you are not causing trouble.

cues: "I am not sure I am even allowed to be here." — say in the opening.
"I see the same things at night." — say if asked what keeps you awake.
"I eat when I can." — say if asked how you are managing.

checkpoints.text: Looks BEYOND the sleeping-tablet request: recognises likely PTSD (nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance) and low mood from trauma/torture, and does NOT simply prescribe sedatives/benzodiazepines — which are inappropriate and not the answer

Reassures him of his ENTITLEMENT: everyone can register with a GP and receive primary care free of charge regardless of immigration status — he is allowed to be here, must not be turned away/charged, and was right to come (countering the fear that deters care)

Recognises and acts on the DESTITUTION/social emergency: not eating, isolation, unclear entitlements — signposting to asylum-support services, food/charitable support, and immigration/legal advice as core parts of the consultation

Takes a TRAUMA-INFORMED approach: unhurried, safe, gently exploring the trauma/mood WITHOUT forcing disclosure; offers appropriate management — sleep hygiene/non-drug measures, and referral to trauma/PTSD services (and specialist torture-survivor services, e.g. Freedom from Torture/Helen Bamber-type services)
Screens mental-health RISK (PTSD-associated depression/suicidality) sensitively and ensures appropriate support/safety-netting
Treats him with DIGNITY and warmth, counters the "I’m a burden"/"not allowed" shame, builds trust, and creates a safe space so he can disclose at his own pace
Avoids re-traumatising or interrogating; follows his lead, validating his experience and his right to care

Safety-nets and follows up: trauma/torture-survivor and mental-health referral, urgent destitution support (asylum support, food, legal advice), sleep advice, crisis routes if risk, an interpreter if needed, and a follow-up appointment to build the relationship — treating the whole person, not the symptom

worked.lbl: Reassure his right to be here
worked.txt: "First, let me put your mind at rest about something really important: you are absolutely allowed to be here and to see me. Everyone can register with a GP and get this care free, whatever their immigration situation. You are not a burden, you are not taking up time you shouldn’t — you did exactly the right thing coming, and I’m glad you did."

"I can give you advice on sleep — but sleeping tablets, especially the strong ones, often aren’t the answer and can cause their own problems. Can I gently ask what’s keeping you awake? … Bad dreams, and feeling on edge. Thank you for telling me. Those can come from very difficult things people have lived through, and there’s real help for that — better help than a tablet."

"You don’t have to tell me anything you’re not ready to — we can go at your pace, today and over time. What you’re describing sounds like the way the mind reacts to trauma, and it’s treatable. I can refer you to people who specialise in helping those who’ve been through what you have."

"Can I also ask — are you managing for food, somewhere to stay, the basics? … I’m really glad you told me. That matters as much as your health, and there’s help I can point you to today — support services for people seeking asylum, food support, and advice about your situation. You shouldn’t be going hungry, and you don’t have to sort this alone."

"When the nights are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living, or think of harming yourself? … Thank you for trusting me. I’ll make sure you have support and numbers to call, and we’ll keep a close eye on how you’re doing."

"So: some practical help for sleep tonight, a referral to the trauma specialists, and I’ll connect you with support for food and your asylum situation today. I’d like to see you again soon — with an interpreter if that’s easier — just to see how you are. You came asking for a small thing and apologising for being here. I want you to leave knowing you’re welcome, you matter, and you’re not on your own."

f.learning: A request for "sleeping tablets" from an asylum seeker is often a presenting ticket over a trauma-and-destitution iceberg. Look beyond it: likely PTSD (nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance) and low mood from torture/persecution and the journey — which needs a trauma-informed approach and referral (including specialist torture-survivor services), NOT sedatives/benzodiazepines. Two equity points are core: reassure his ENTITLEMENT (everyone can register with a GP and receive primary care free of charge regardless of immigration status — he must not be turned away or charged, and was right to come), countering the fear that deters vulnerable people from care; and recognise the DESTITUTION as a social emergency (not eating, isolation, unclear entitlements) needing urgent signposting to asylum-support, food and legal advice. The examinable hidden agenda is profound, not-yet-voiced trauma plus shame, fear of authority, and destitution he is too proud to disclose ("I don’t want to be a burden"); create safety and dignity, open the door gently without forcing disclosure, screen mental-health risk, and follow up to build trust — treating the whole person, not the symptom.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE TA77 (hypnotics for insomnia, 2004) · NHS England patient registration standard operating principles · NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 · Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 (asylum support)
knowledge.summary: A request for sleeping tablets from a newly registered man seeking asylum is the entry point to probable PTSD and destitution. Confirm his right to free GP care, gently explore trauma symptoms and risk, do not make a hypnotic the answer, refer for trauma-focused therapy, and act on food, money and legal advice today.

points.h: He is entitled to be here
points.t: Anyone in England can register with a GP practice and receive primary care free of charge. NHS England’s registration principles say practices should not refuse registration because a person cannot show ID, proof of address or immigration status. People with an active asylum claim are also exempt from hospital charges under the NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015.

points.h: The request is a ticket, not the problem
points.t: Poor sleep here sits on nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance. Hypnotics do not treat PTSD. NICE TA77 limits Z-drugs to severe insomnia for the shortest time, and the BNF restricts benzodiazepines to short courses because of dependence. NICE NG116 advises against drug treatment, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD.

Re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood after trauma such as torture or a dangerous journey. NICE NG116: trauma-focused CBT for adults; EMDR is recommended for PTSD after non-combat trauma. Consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if he prefers medication. Specialist torture-survivor services add expertise.

NICE NG116 advises building in extra time to develop trust with people who have complex PTSD, and taking account of the safety and stability of their circumstances, such as housing and money. Hunger and fear of removal make trauma work impossible; addressing them is part of the treatment.

Destitute asylum seekers can apply for Home Office asylum support under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 (section 98 emergency support, section 95 ongoing support), through the Migrant Help advice line. Those on support can get an HC2 certificate for free prescriptions. Add food bank vouchers, British Red Cross or local refugee charities, and immigration legal advice.

points.h: Ask about risk, with an interpreter if needed
points.t: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and self-neglect; NICE NG225 advises against risk scales to decide care. Use a professional interpreter rather than friends or family whenever language is a barrier (NHS England interpreting guidance for primary care, 2018).

dg.d: Reassured his right to free GP care first, then used an open question about the nights before narrowing.
Food, shelter, isolation, knowledge of entitlements and fear of authority, asked gently and without judgement.
Mood and PTSD symptom review, weight and nutrition at the next face-to-face contact, and a new-patient health review with interpreter if needed.
Primary insomnia versus PTSD, depression, and the physical effects of hunger and poor sleep.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and protective factors; considered self-neglect from not eating.
Named probable PTSD with trauma-related insomnia and destitution, in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No hypnotic as the answer; trauma-focused therapy referral (NICE NG116) including torture-survivor services; medication offered as a choice; non-drug sleep measures.
Asylum support via Migrant Help, food bank, legal advice, HC2 route; interpreter offered.
Crisis routes named (999, NHS 111 mental health option), review in two weeks, referrals chased.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I don’t want to be a burden”, “not sure I’m allowed” and watching the door, and explored each.
What he hoped the tablets would do, his shame about asking, and his fear of being judged or sent away.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — That you are not allowed to see a doctor, that you will be a burden or reported. Underneath: the memories, and having no food or money — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Bekele, I’m Dr Lee. Before anything else, you asked whether you are allowed to be here. You are. Everyone can register with a GP and see us free of charge, whatever their immigration situation. You did the right thing booking.
model.why: Answers the entitlement fear first, because it governs everything else

model.text: Thank you. I did not know. I am sorry to take your time. I only need something for the sleep.

You’re not taking anyone’s time — this appointment is yours. I do want to help with the sleep. Could we spend a few minutes on how things are for you, and then decide together what will actually help? Is it all right to talk in English, or would an interpreter make it easier?
model.why: Sets a shared agenda and offers an interpreter

model.text: English is okay. Yes, we can talk.
Tell me about the nights. What happens when you try to sleep?
model.why: Open question that follows his agenda before widening it

model.text: I lie down and my mind does not stop. When I sleep, the bad dreams come. I wake and I am wet, my heart is fast. Then I stay awake until morning.
That sounds exhausting and frightening. You don’t have to tell me what the dreams are about. Can I ask — during the day, do memories ever push in when you don’t want them, as if it’s happening again?
model.why: Screens for re-experiencing without asking for trauma content

model.text: Yes. A sudden noise, and I am back there. I do not go where there are many people. I watch the door always.

Thank you for trusting me with that. Flashbacks, avoiding crowds, always being on guard — the mind often reacts this way after very frightening experiences. We can go at your pace today; you choose what to share.
model.why: Validates, names the pattern, and gives him control over disclosure

model.text: Some things I cannot say yet.
That’s completely fine. Can I ask about the everyday things — are you managing for food, and somewhere safe to stay?
model.why: Moves gently to the social emergency that he will not raise himself

model.text: I… sometimes I do not eat. One meal, some days nothing. I do not want to ask. I do not want to be a burden to anyone.
I’m really glad you told me. Hunger isn’t something to be ashamed of, and it matters to your health as much as your sleep. Do you know what support you can get while your claim is being decided?
model.why: Removes shame and checks his knowledge before advising

model.text: No. I am not sure what I am allowed. I am afraid if I ask, they will think badly of me, or send me away.
When the nights are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living, or have thoughts of harming yourself?
model.why: Asks directly about suicide risk in plain words

model.text: Sometimes I think it would be easier to sleep and not wake. But I would not do anything. I still have hope.

Thank you for being honest — that took courage. I’m glad you have hope. If those thoughts ever get stronger or you start to plan anything, I need you to contact us or the crisis line straight away. Will you do that?
model.why: Clarifies passive ideation, protective factors and a crisis agreement

model.text: Yes, I will.
You came hoping for sleeping tablets. What did you imagine they would do for you?
model.why: Explores his idea and expectation rather than refusing outright

model.text: Just to stop the thinking. To rest. So I can be strong for my case.

That makes complete sense. Here is my honest view. The sleep problem looks like part of something bigger — the nightmares, the flashbacks and being on guard fit a condition called post-traumatic stress. It’s common after what people fleeing danger go through, and it is treatable.
model.why: Gives a clear working diagnosis in plain language

model.text: It has a name? I thought I was becoming weak in the mind.

It has a name, and it’s a normal reaction to abnormal events, not weakness. Strong sleeping tablets don’t treat it. They can become hard to stop and make you feel foggy, which matters when you need a clear head for your case. The treatment that works best is a talking therapy that focuses on the trauma, with people trained in this.
model.why: Explains why hypnotics are not the answer and what does work

model.text: But I will have to talk about everything?

Only when you feel ready, and with someone skilled. There are services that specialise in helping people who have survived torture or persecution — they go at your pace. If you’d prefer, a daily medicine for the nightmares and anxiety is also an option we can talk about next time.
model.why: Addresses the fear of forced disclosure and offers choice

model.text: Okay. That sounds better than I thought.

For today, I’d like to do three things. First, a referral for trauma support, including a specialist service for survivors. Second — and this can’t wait — help with food and money: there’s Home Office support for people seeking asylum who have nothing, and a free advice line, Migrant Help, that helps you apply. I can give you a food bank voucher today and the details of a refugee charity near you.
model.why: Acts on destitution as part of the medical plan

model.text: They will not think I am taking what is not mine?

No. This support exists for exactly your situation. Asking for it is not being a burden. I’d also suggest free immigration legal advice — a charity can point you to it. And if you get asylum support you can apply for a certificate that makes prescriptions free.
model.why: Links him to legal advice and the HC2 route

model.text: For the nights themselves: a regular getting-up time, no caffeine after midday, and if you wake from a nightmare, get up, put a light on, name where you are and the date, and ground yourself before lying back down. Does that feel doable?
model.why: Practical non-drug sleep advice he can use tonight, then checks acceptability

model.text: Yes. I can try this.
Before we finish — what will you do tomorrow as your first step?
model.why: Teach-back that checks the plan has landed

model.text: Call the number, Migrant Help. Go to the food place with your paper. Wait for the trauma service letter.

Exactly right. If the dark thoughts get stronger, or you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’d like to see you again in two weeks, face to face or by video — with an interpreter if you’d like — to see how you are and chase the referrals. Is that all right?
model.why: Specific crisis routes and a booked review to build trust

model.text: Yes. Thank you, doctor. I came for a small thing. You were kind to me.
You were right to come, and you’re welcome here. We’ll take this step by step together.

social.t: Skipping meals, no money and no network. Hunger worsens sleep, mood and concentration, and shame stops him asking. Ask directly and normalise help-seeking.
People seeking asylum may fear that contact with services affects their claim. Explain what the consultation is for and how his information is kept confidential.

legal.t: Registration and primary care are free for everyone in England regardless of immigration status; ID, address or status documents are not required to register (NHS England registration principles). Asylum seekers with an active claim are exempt from hospital charges (NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015).

Destitute asylum seekers can apply for Home Office support under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999: section 98 (emergency) and section 95 (ongoing). Migrant Help runs the free advice and application line.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): treat patients fairly and without discrimination, and support them to access care. Record disclosures factually and only what he consents to share.
Offer a professional interpreter for future contacts; avoid family or community members, especially for trauma disclosure (NHS England interpreting guidance, 2018).
Hypnotics carry dependence risk and do not treat PTSD (BNF; NICE TA77; NICE NG116). Declining one is safe practice if it comes with a better alternative.

community.t: Freedom from Torture and the Helen Bamber Foundation (survivors of torture and trafficking); Refugee Council; British Red Cross refugee services; Doctors of the World; local food banks; Migrant Help for asylum support.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans or preparation — ask directly and clarify protective factors
Not eating or drinking enough: weight loss, weakness, self-neglect
Severe PTSD features or dissociation that stop him functioning safely
Physical effects of past torture or the journey (pain, injuries) that may need assessment later
psychosocial: Food, shelter, money and whether he knows about asylum support
Isolation, faith and any sources of support or hope
Fear of authority and of being seen as a burden or sent away
ice: Idea: “I just need something to help me sleep”
Concern: not being allowed to see a doctor; shame at asking; trauma he is not ready to voice
Expectation: a prescription and to leave quickly without troubling anyone

playbook.diagnosis: Probable post-traumatic stress disorder presenting as insomnia, with low mood and destitution: “The nightmares, the flashbacks and always being on guard fit post-traumatic stress, a common and treatable reaction to very frightening experiences.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your mind has been through things no one should, and it’s stuck on high alert — like a smoke alarm that keeps going off long after the fire. Sleeping tablets just cover the noise. The right help teaches the alarm to settle.”

management.reflectIce: “You came asking for tablets so you could rest and be strong for your case. That’s exactly what I want for you too — and there’s better help for that than a tablet.”
management.psychosocial: Treat hunger and uncertainty as part of the illness: asylum support through Migrant Help, a food bank voucher, legal advice and an HC2 certificate, so trauma therapy has a stable base.
sharedPlan: Refer for trauma-focused therapy (NICE NG116) and to a specialist torture-survivor service; offer medication as a choice later
Non-drug sleep and grounding advice for nightmares; no hypnotic as the answer
Asylum support, food and legal advice today; interpreter offered for future appointments
safetyNet: Suicidal thoughts getting stronger or any plan: 999, or NHS 111 mental health option, and contact the practice
Review in two weeks to check safety, food and referrals, building trust over time

pitfalls.intro: This station is not about hypnotic pharmacology. It is failed by accepting the ticket, by missing the man behind it, and by treating hunger and fear as someone else’s job. Each pattern below is common in examiner feedback and fixable.

items.fail: Issuing a week of zopiclone “just to help him settle”, or refusing any help and ending the call.
items.why: Either response misses probable PTSD. Hypnotics do not treat it and carry dependence risk (NICE TA77; BNF); a bare refusal leaves him with nothing.
items.fix: Decline the tablet by offering something better: “Strong sleeping tablets don’t treat what’s keeping you awake — there’s a treatment that does.”

items.fail: Skipping past “I’m not sure I’m allowed to be here”.
items.why: His fear of ineligibility shapes everything he says next. Leaving it unanswered keeps him guarded and minimising.
items.fix: Answer it in the first minute: “You are allowed to be here. GP care is free for everyone, whatever their immigration situation.”

items.fail: Asking him to describe what happened to him in detail to “confirm the diagnosis”.
items.why: Interrogating trauma can re-traumatise and is not needed to recognise PTSD or refer. Examiners mark this as poor Relating.
items.fix: Ask about symptoms, not the story: nightmares, intrusive memories, avoidance, being on guard. “You choose what to share.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he is eating or has money, because it is “not medical”.
items.why: Destitution is a core part of this case. NICE NG116 notes stability and safety matter before trauma work.
items.fix: Ask directly and act today: Migrant Help for asylum support, a food bank voucher, legal advice, HC2.

items.fail: No question about suicide in a traumatised, isolated, hungry man with insomnia.
items.why: Missing risk assessment is a serious Tasks omission. His passive thoughts are only found if you ask.
items.fix: “When nights are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living?” Then clarify plans, protective factors and crisis routes.

items.fail: A list of charity names read out at speed, with no follow-up booked.
items.why: Unprioritised signposting to a frightened patient rarely leads to action; examiners flag “no clear follow-up”.
items.fix: Agree one or two first steps, check them with teach-back, and book a review in two weeks with an interpreter offered.

Nightmares and waking; intrusive memories and avoidance (without asking for the story); food and shelter; suicide risk.

timeMap.h: Hear his hope for the tablets
timeMap.d: “What did you imagine they would do?” — rest, a clear head for his case. Use it to frame the plan.
Probable PTSD, why hypnotics don’t help, trauma-focused therapy and torture-survivor services, then asylum support, food and legal advice today.
Crisis routes in plain words, teach-back of the first step, review in two weeks with an interpreter if wanted.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a hypnotic or refuses flatly and ends; never addresses whether he is allowed to be seen; misses the nightmares and flashbacks; never asks about food or risk; hurries a man who is already apologising for existing.
wordPics.pass: Reassures entitlement, recognises probable PTSD, explains why tablets aren’t the answer, refers for trauma therapy, asks about suicide risk, and signposts asylum support and food with a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: lets him set the pace of disclosure, removes the shame of asking for help, gives concrete first steps (Migrant Help, food voucher, legal advice, HC2), uses teach-back, offers an interpreter, and he leaves feeling welcome rather than processed.

Thank you for trusting me with that. Flashbacks, avoiding crowds, always being on guard — the mind often reacts this way after very frightening experiences. We can go at your pace today; you choose what to share.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates, names the pattern, and gives him control over disclosure

SCA_MODELS.text: Some things I cannot say yet.
That’s completely fine. Can I ask about the everyday things — are you managing for food, and somewhere safe to stay?
SCA_MODELS.why: Moves gently to the social emergency that he will not raise himself

SCA_MODELS.text: I… sometimes I do not eat. One meal, some days nothing. I do not want to ask. I do not want to be a burden to anyone.
I’m really glad you told me. Hunger isn’t something to be ashamed of, and it matters to your health as much as your sleep. Do you know what support you can get while your claim is being decided?
SCA_MODELS.why: Removes shame and checks his knowledge before advising

SCA_MODELS.text: No. I am not sure what I am allowed. I am afraid if I ask, they will think badly of me, or send me away.
When the nights are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living, or have thoughts of harming yourself?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks directly about suicide risk in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: Sometimes I think it would be easier to sleep and not wake. But I would not do anything. I still have hope.

Thank you for being honest — that took courage. I’m glad you have hope. If those thoughts ever get stronger or you start to plan anything, I need you to contact us or the crisis line straight away. Will you do that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Clarifies passive ideation, protective factors and a crisis agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I will.
You came hoping for sleeping tablets. What did you imagine they would do for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores his idea and expectation rather than refusing outright

SCA_MODELS.text: Just to stop the thinking. To rest. So I can be strong for my case.

That makes complete sense. Here is my honest view. The sleep problem looks like part of something bigger — the nightmares, the flashbacks and being on guard fit a condition called post-traumatic stress. It’s common after what people fleeing danger go through, and it is treatable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives a clear working diagnosis in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: It has a name? I thought I was becoming weak in the mind.

It has a name, and it’s a normal reaction to abnormal events, not weakness. Strong sleeping tablets don’t treat it. They can become hard to stop and make you feel foggy, which matters when you need a clear head for your case. The treatment that works best is a talking therapy that focuses on the trauma, with people trained in this.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why hypnotics are not the answer and what does work

SCA_MODELS.text: But I will have to talk about everything?

Only when you feel ready, and with someone skilled. There are services that specialise in helping people who have survived torture or persecution — they go at your pace. If you’d prefer, a daily medicine for the nightmares and anxiety is also an option we can talk about next time.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the fear of forced disclosure and offers choice

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That sounds better than I thought.

For today, I’d like to do three things. First, a referral for trauma support, including a specialist service for survivors. Second — and this can’t wait — help with food and money: there’s Home Office support for people seeking asylum who have nothing, and a free advice line, Migrant Help, that helps you apply. I can give you a food bank voucher today and the details of a refugee charity near you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acts on destitution as part of the medical plan

SCA_MODELS.text: They will not think I am taking what is not mine?

No. This support exists for exactly your situation. Asking for it is not being a burden. I’d also suggest free immigration legal advice — a charity can point you to it. And if you get asylum support you can apply for a certificate that makes prescriptions free.
SCA_MODELS.why: Links him to legal advice and the HC2 route

SCA_MODELS.text: For the nights themselves: a regular getting-up time, no caffeine after midday, and if you wake from a nightmare, get up, put a light on, name where you are and the date, and ground yourself before lying back down. Does that feel doable?
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical non-drug sleep advice he can use tonight, then checks acceptability

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I can try this.
Before we finish — what will you do tomorrow as your first step?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back that checks the plan has landed

SCA_MODELS.text: Call the number, Migrant Help. Go to the food place with your paper. Wait for the trauma service letter.

Exactly right. If the dark thoughts get stronger, or you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’d like to see you again in two weeks, face to face or by video — with an interpreter if you’d like — to see how you are and chase the referrals. Is that all right?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific crisis routes and a booked review to build trust

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. Thank you, doctor. I came for a small thing. You were kind to me.
You were right to come, and you’re welcome here. We’ll take this step by step together.

SCA_STEM.name: Tesfaye Bekele
pmh: Recorded at registration as seeking asylum
SCA_STEM.recent: Registration completed recently. No previous consultations with the practice and no new-patient health review yet.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked a video appointment for “sleeping tablets”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE TA77 (hypnotics for insomnia, 2004) · NHS England patient registration standard operating principles · NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 · Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 (asylum support)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A request for sleeping tablets from a newly registered man seeking asylum is the entry point to probable PTSD and destitution. Confirm his right to free GP care, gently explore trauma symptoms and risk, do not make a hypnotic the answer, refer for trauma-focused therapy, and act on food, money and legal advice today.

points.h: He is entitled to be here
points.t: Anyone in England can register with a GP practice and receive primary care free of charge. NHS England’s registration principles say practices should not refuse registration because a person cannot show ID, proof of address or immigration status. People with an active asylum claim are also exempt from hospital charges under the NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015.

points.h: The request is a ticket, not the problem
points.t: Poor sleep here sits on nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance. Hypnotics do not treat PTSD. NICE TA77 limits Z-drugs to severe insomnia for the shortest time, and the BNF restricts benzodiazepines to short courses because of dependence. NICE NG116 advises against drug treatment, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD.

Re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood after trauma such as torture or a dangerous journey. NICE NG116: trauma-focused CBT for adults; EMDR is recommended for PTSD after non-combat trauma. Consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if he prefers medication. Specialist torture-survivor services add expertise.

NICE NG116 advises building in extra time to develop trust with people who have complex PTSD, and taking account of the safety and stability of their circumstances, such as housing and money. Hunger and fear of removal make trauma work impossible; addressing them is part of the treatment.

Destitute asylum seekers can apply for Home Office asylum support under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 (section 98 emergency support, section 95 ongoing support), through the Migrant Help advice line. Those on support can get an HC2 certificate for free prescriptions. Add food bank vouchers, British Red Cross or local refugee charities, and immigration legal advice.

points.h: Ask about risk, with an interpreter if needed
points.t: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and self-neglect; NICE NG225 advises against risk scales to decide care. Use a professional interpreter rather than friends or family whenever language is a barrier (NHS England interpreting guidance for primary care, 2018).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Reassured his right to free GP care first, then used an open question about the nights before narrowing.
Food, shelter, isolation, knowledge of entitlements and fear of authority, asked gently and without judgement.
Picked up “I don’t want to be a burden”, “not sure I’m allowed” and watching the door, and explored each.
What he hoped the tablets would do, his shame about asking, and his fear of being judged or sent away.
Mood and PTSD symptom review, weight and nutrition at the next face-to-face contact, and a new-patient health review with interpreter if needed.
Primary insomnia versus PTSD, depression, and the physical effects of hunger and poor sleep.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and protective factors; considered self-neglect from not eating.
Named probable PTSD with trauma-related insomnia and destitution, in plain words.
No hypnotic as the answer; trauma-focused therapy referral (NICE NG116) including torture-survivor services; medication offered as a choice; non-drug sleep measures.
Asylum support via Migrant Help, food bank, legal advice, HC2 route; interpreter offered.
Crisis routes named (999, NHS 111 mental health option), review in two weeks, referrals chased.

social.t: Skipping meals, no money and no network. Hunger worsens sleep, mood and concentration, and shame stops him asking. Ask directly and normalise help-seeking.
People seeking asylum may fear that contact with services affects their claim. Explain what the consultation is for and how his information is kept confidential.

legal.t: Registration and primary care are free for everyone in England regardless of immigration status; ID, address or status documents are not required to register (NHS England registration principles). Asylum seekers with an active claim are exempt from hospital charges (NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015).

Destitute asylum seekers can apply for Home Office support under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999: section 98 (emergency) and section 95 (ongoing). Migrant Help runs the free advice and application line.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): treat patients fairly and without discrimination, and support them to access care. Record disclosures factually and only what he consents to share.
Offer a professional interpreter for future contacts; avoid family or community members, especially for trauma disclosure (NHS England interpreting guidance, 2018).
Hypnotics carry dependence risk and do not treat PTSD (BNF; NICE TA77; NICE NG116). Declining one is safe practice if it comes with a better alternative.

community.t: Freedom from Torture and the Helen Bamber Foundation (survivors of torture and trafficking); Refugee Council; British Red Cross refugee services; Doctors of the World; local food banks; Migrant Help for asylum support.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans or preparation — ask directly and clarify protective factors
Not eating or drinking enough: weight loss, weakness, self-neglect
Severe PTSD features or dissociation that stop him functioning safely
Physical effects of past torture or the journey (pain, injuries) that may need assessment later
psychosocial: Food, shelter, money and whether he knows about asylum support
Isolation, faith and any sources of support or hope
Fear of authority and of being seen as a burden or sent away
ice: Idea: “I just need something to help me sleep”
Concern: not being allowed to see a doctor; shame at asking; trauma he is not ready to voice
Expectation: a prescription and to leave quickly without troubling anyone

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable post-traumatic stress disorder presenting as insomnia, with low mood and destitution: “The nightmares, the flashbacks and always being on guard fit post-traumatic stress, a common and treatable reaction to very frightening experiences.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your mind has been through things no one should, and it’s stuck on high alert — like a smoke alarm that keeps going off long after the fire. Sleeping tablets just cover the noise. The right help teaches the alarm to settle.”

management.reflectIce: “You came asking for tablets so you could rest and be strong for your case. That’s exactly what I want for you too — and there’s better help for that than a tablet.”
management.psychosocial: Treat hunger and uncertainty as part of the illness: asylum support through Migrant Help, a food bank voucher, legal advice and an HC2 certificate, so trauma therapy has a stable base.
sharedPlan: Refer for trauma-focused therapy (NICE NG116) and to a specialist torture-survivor service; offer medication as a choice later
Non-drug sleep and grounding advice for nightmares; no hypnotic as the answer
Asylum support, food and legal advice today; interpreter offered for future appointments
safetyNet: Suicidal thoughts getting stronger or any plan: 999, or NHS 111 mental health option, and contact the practice
Review in two weeks to check safety, food and referrals, building trust over time

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not about hypnotic pharmacology. It is failed by accepting the ticket, by missing the man behind it, and by treating hunger and fear as someone else’s job. Each pattern below is common in examiner feedback and fixable.

items.fail: Issuing a week of zopiclone “just to help him settle”, or refusing any help and ending the call.
items.why: Either response misses probable PTSD. Hypnotics do not treat it and carry dependence risk (NICE TA77; BNF); a bare refusal leaves him with nothing.
items.fix: Decline the tablet by offering something better: “Strong sleeping tablets don’t treat what’s keeping you awake — there’s a treatment that does.”

items.fail: Skipping past “I’m not sure I’m allowed to be here”.
items.why: His fear of ineligibility shapes everything he says next. Leaving it unanswered keeps him guarded and minimising.
items.fix: Answer it in the first minute: “You are allowed to be here. GP care is free for everyone, whatever their immigration situation.”

items.fail: Asking him to describe what happened to him in detail to “confirm the diagnosis”.
items.why: Interrogating trauma can re-traumatise and is not needed to recognise PTSD or refer. Examiners mark this as poor Relating.
items.fix: Ask about symptoms, not the story: nightmares, intrusive memories, avoidance, being on guard. “You choose what to share.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he is eating or has money, because it is “not medical”.
items.why: Destitution is a core part of this case. NICE NG116 notes stability and safety matter before trauma work.
items.fix: Ask directly and act today: Migrant Help for asylum support, a food bank voucher, legal advice, HC2.

items.fail: No question about suicide in a traumatised, isolated, hungry man with insomnia.
items.why: Missing risk assessment is a serious Tasks omission. His passive thoughts are only found if you ask.
items.fix: “When nights are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living?” Then clarify plans, protective factors and crisis routes.

items.fail: A list of charity names read out at speed, with no follow-up booked.
items.why: Unprioritised signposting to a frightened patient rarely leads to action; examiners flag “no clear follow-up”.
items.fix: Agree one or two first steps, check them with teach-back, and book a review in two weeks with an interpreter offered.
